deep.reconstruction:
CONTEXT. This is a working sheet from Gauss's determination of the orbit of Vesta, discovered by Olbers on 29 March 1807. It has four parts: (A) the Sun's place for 6 April, 3 April and 8 April, taken from solar tables; (B) the reduction of a ring-micrometer observation of Vesta on 8 April; (C) a smoothed daily ephemeris of Vesta for 29 March - 9 April with observed-minus-ephemeris residuals; (D) scattered auxiliary items: two later positions for 12 and 14 April, and a small quadratic.

(A) SONNENORT APRIL 6.
1. Mean quantities. Epoch row: 8 deg 16'27.10", followed by table arguments 7462.90, 769, 658, 684, 297. The motion for 6 days is added: 5 deg 54'49.98", 164.27, 203, 10, 15, 1. The sums are 14 deg 11'17.08", 7627.17, (1)972, 668, 699, 298.
 - The epoch is the same instant 6.000 days before. Check: 5 deg 54'49.98" / 0.9856473 deg per day = 6.000 days, i.e. 59'08.33" per day. The same holds for 3 April (2 deg 57'24.99" = 3 days) and 8 April (7 deg 53'06.64" = 8 days). The epoch is therefore 'April 0'.
 - The first argument grows by 27.378 per day, i.e. 10000 per year: it is the Sun's anomaly in parts of 10000.
 - The others grow by about 33.8 per day (lunar, synodic month), about 1.7 per day (Venus, about 584 days) and 2.5 per day (Jupiter, about 399 days). The last is slow (Mars or a long-period term; my identification).
2. Longitude. Mean value 14 deg 11'17.08", plus the equation of centre +1 deg 54'54.48", minus 1.37", gives 16 deg 06'10.19". Then add four small corrections:
 - -1.32" (lunar term);
 - -10.46" (nutation in longitude);
 - +8.29" (planetary terms);
 - +37.18" (a constant table correction, nearly constant on all dates).
 The result is the apparent longitude L = 16 deg 06'43.88".
3. Radius vector. Table value 1.0016199, corrections +361 -39 +17 (units 1e-7), giving R = 1.0016538 and log R = 0.0007176.
4. Obliquity. Mean 23 deg 27'52.87", nutation -2.84", true obliquity eps = 23 deg 27'50.03".
5. Logarithms (10 added to characteristics):
 - log cos L = 9.9825969;
 - log(R cos eps) = 9.9632343;
 - log sin L = 9.4432928;
 - log(R sin eps) = 9.6007872.
6. Equatorial rectangular coordinates of the Sun:
 - X = R cos L = +0.9623089;
 - Y = R sin L cos eps = +0.2549923;
 - Z = R sin L sin eps = +0.1106828.
 These are the solar coordinates needed for the geocentric-heliocentric reduction in the orbit determination.

SONNENORT APRIL 3 (same scheme, 3 days).
 - Arguments: 11 deg 13'52.09", 7545.03, 871, 663, 692.
 - Longitude: +1 deg 55'19.47" -1.38" gives 13 deg 09'10.18". Then -5.44 -10.50 +8.36 +37.20 gives L = 13 deg 09'39.80".
 - Radius: 1.0007567 +252 -28 +5 = 1.0007796, log = 0.0003384.

SONNENORT APRIL 8 (8 days).
 - Arguments: 16 deg 09'33.74", 7681.92, (1)040, 672, 704, 298.
 - Longitude: +1 deg 54'24.66" -1.36" gives 18 deg 03'57.04". Then +1.87 -10.42 +8.22 +37.18 gives L = 18 deg 04'33.89".
 - Radius: 1.0021930 +355 -47 +25 = 1.0022263, log = 0.0009658.
 - The X, Y, Z for 3 and 8 April are not carried out on this page.

(B) VESTA, 8 APRIL, RING (CIRCLE) MICROMETER.
1. Data. Seven passages, each with clock time, star entry/exit (0 : 105.5, etc.) and Vesta entry/exit (261 : 367, etc.), in seconds.
2. Right-ascension difference. This is the difference of chord midpoints, (Ve_in + Ve_out)/2 - (St_in + St_out)/2. The seven values are 261.25, 260.25, 261.25, 260.75, 259.75, 259.50, 259.25; their simple mean is 260.29 s.
 - Gauss writes 'sequitur 260.83'. Converted from mean to sidereal time (x 1.0027379) and to arc (x 15), this gives 3923.2" = 1 deg 05'23.2".
 - Added to the comparison star's apparent RA, 180 deg 51'27.46" (computed on the previous page), it gives Vesta RA = 181 deg 56'50.7". Gauss has 181 deg 56'51.0"; the 0.3" can come from the star's apparent place on 8 April.
3. Declination. From the chord lengths Vesta is 'nordlich 33.5"' of the star: 12 deg 35'28.91" + 33.5" = 12 deg 36'02.4" (Gauss 12 deg 36'02.3").
4. Final line. 'M.Z. 8h28m49s 181 deg 56'51.0" 12 deg 35'45.8"' carries a further -16.5" in declination. Compare the marginal 'Subtr. von d. Decl. 14.9' (previous page); its exact origin is unclear. 'Uhrzeit 8h20'7.5", 8h30'40"' is a clock-time to mean-time comparison.

(C) EPHEMERIS AND RESIDUALS (column 'Observ.').
1. The RA series 29 March - 9 April has first differences -835.0, -825.5, -816.2, ..., -741.3" and almost constant second differences of +9.3 to +9.5". It is a smoothed (interpolated) ephemeris.
2. The adjacent column gives observed minus ephemeris:
 - 29 March: 184 deg 08'34.7" - 34.0" = +0.7;
 - 30 March: 36.8 - 39.0 = -2.2;
 - 1 April: +1.2; 2 April: +1.8; 3 April: 0; 4 April: -2.0;
 - 5 April (Harding 182 deg 34'27.8"): +1.6;
 - 6 April: mean of 182 deg 21'31.2" and Harding 41.6" = 36.4", against 36.9" gives -0.5;
 - 8 April: values 32.6", 20.3" and Olbers 23.1". The mean of the first two is 26.4"; the mean of all three, 25.3", against 26.4" gives -1.1.
3. The declination series behaves the same way, with second differences of about -15.0". Residuals: 0, -7.6, +10.3, +5.7, 0, +10.3, +7.8, +10.9.
4. On 8 April the declinations of Olbers (12 deg 36'18.8"), Gauss (36'7.8") and Harding (35'52.8") are bracketed with '8.1'. Their simple mean is 12 deg 36'06.5", so the 8.1 is not reproduced.

(D) AUXILIARY ITEMS.
 - Positions for 12 April (181 deg 09'19.3", 12 deg 48'34.1") and 14 April (180 deg 47'20.3", 12 deg 53'06.4"). These are not a quadratic extrapolation of the series (that would give about 181 deg 07'57" for 12 April). They are presumably later observations or orbit-computed places, used on the next page together with 'Sonnenort April 10 u. 14' and the elements (node 108 deg 31', inclination 7 deg 23').
 - A three-point quadratic: f(0) = 0, f(5) = 0, f(10) = -5.6, written 'x.(x-5).0,112'. In magnitude f(x) = 0.112 x (x-5), which is 5.6 at x = 10, so the intended form is f = -0.112 x (x-5). This is a quadratic correction curve through three normal points.
errors: Equation of centre for 6 April (1 deg 54'54.48") is inconsistent with the neighbouring dates. With arguments 7545.03, 7627.17, 7681.92, 7736.68, 7846.19, 7955.70 and values 1 deg 55'19.47", 54'54.48", 54'24.66", 53'48.74", 52'12.62", 50'05.30", the second divided differences are about -0.00130 to -0.00135 except around 6 April (-0.00176 and -0.00102). Lowering the 6 April value by about 1.9" (to about 1 deg 54'52.5") restores smoothness. The Sun's longitude for 6 April should then be about 16 deg 06'42.0" rather than 43.88" (probable slip of about 2"; the X, Y, Z are computed consistently from the value written).

Declination ephemeris for 30 March, 11 deg 53'42.6", breaks the otherwise perfect second differences (-15.0"). The smooth value is 11 deg 53'22.6" (first difference 5'58.9" rather than 6'18.9"). The residual -7.6" for 30 March (observed 11 deg 53'35.0") should then be about +12.4". This looks like a 20" slip by Gauss.
Declination residual for 1 April is +10.3", but the observed 12 deg 04'48.8" (previous page) minus the ephemeris 12 deg 04'35.5" gives +13.3". Either a 3" slip or a different observed value was used.
The RA difference 'sequitur 260.83 s' does not equal the simple mean of the seven midpoint differences (260.29 s); the reduction used is not shown.

The arc written '1 deg 5' 33.2"' cannot be right if 181 deg 56'51.0" was obtained from the star at 180 deg 51'27.46". The required value, and the sidereal conversion of 260.83 s, is 1 deg 05'23.2". Either a misreading or a slip of the pen.
The bracketed '8.1' for the three 8 April declinations does not equal their mean (12 deg 36'06.5"); its meaning is unclear.

results.what: Apparent solar longitude, radius vector and equatorial rectangular solar coordinates (X, Y, Z) from solar tables, with equation of centre, lunar and planetary perturbations, nutation and obliquity
results.modern_name: Computation of geocentric equatorial solar coordinates from solar tables (ephemeris computation)
results.usually_credited_to: Standard practice c. 1800 (solar tables of Delambre / von Zach)

results.what: Differential right ascension and declination of Vesta relative to a comparison star from transit chords across a ring micrometer, with mean-to-sidereal conversion
Smoothed daily ephemeris with constant second differences, and observed-minus-computed residuals for observations by Gauss, Olbers and Harding
results.modern_name: Smoothing by finite differences / O-C residual analysis

deep.surprise_reason: These are routine working computations (solar places, micrometer reduction, ephemeris smoothing) in Gauss's well-documented 1807 orbit determination of Vesta. Their only interest is documentary, including a few small slips.

log(R cos eps) = 9.9632343 and log(R sin eps) = 9.6007872

RA ephemeris second differences are all about +9.3 to +9.5"

transcription_corrections: Declination for 30 March reads '11.53.42,6' (digits overwritten). Arithmetically the ephemeris should be 11.53.22,6, but the written 42,6 is consistent with Gauss's residual -7.6, so it is Gauss's own slip rather than a misreading.
'sequitur 260''83 = 1° 5' 33''2': the arc should be 1° 5' 23''2 to reproduce 181.56.51,0. The last digits are overwritten in the image; check whether '23' or '32' is written.
In the April 6 head, '9. 8.16.27,10' has the '9.' and the first entry struck through. Similarly '1,0016199' has its last digits overwritten.
April 14 RA '180.47.20,3' has overwritten seconds in the image (possibly corrected from another value).
The minus sign before the 3 April lunar term ('-5,44') is written over a struck-out entry.
In the declination block on the right, '12°' is a column header for the 8 April declinations of Olbers, Gauss and Harding (12°36'18.8", 12°36'7.8", 12°35'52.8").
